p.x:
Last Saturday, my class went to the zoo. First, we saw the lions. They were sleeping in the sun. Then we watched the monkeys. One monkey took a boy's hat and ran away! Everyone laughed.
Next, we visited the bear. It was big and brown. In the insect house, there were bees, a huge spider and many beautiful butterflies. My friend was scared of the spider, but I thought it was interesting.
In the evening, we heard an owl and some frogs near the lake. It was a great day. I want to work with animals when I grow up.

Khao Yai, Thailand's first national park, is home to an amazing variety of wildlife. The park covers more than 2,000 square kilometres of jungle and grassland.
Visitors often see deer and monkeys near the roads, and wild elephants sometimes cross in front of cars! If you're lucky, you might hear gibbons calling in the morning or see a hornbill flying overhead. Hornbills build their nest in holes high in old trees. The park is also home to leopards and black bears, which have long, sharp claws, though they are rarely seen. Near the rivers, there may even be crocodiles.
Park rangers work hard to protect the animals. One of their biggest problems is poachers, who hunt animals illegally. Some sell animal parts in the illegal trade. In the past, elephants were killed for their ivory, and in other parts of Asia, rhinos are still hunted for their horns.
Another threat is habitat loss. When forests are cut down for farms or roads, animals lose their homes, and many species face extinction. Herbivores, like deer, depend on plants, while carnivores, like tigers, depend on herbivores. If one part of the food chain disappears, the whole system suffers. That's why reserves like Khao Yai are so important: many animals there are threatened.

Scientists warn that the world is experiencing a dramatic decline in wildlife. Populations of mammals, birds, fish and reptiles have fallen sharply since 1970, driven mainly by habitat loss, pollution, climate change and trafficking. The pangolin, a small scaly animal from Asia and Africa, is believed to be the most trafficked mammal in the world.
Conservationists use a variety of tools to fight back. Camera traps, hidden in forests, record images of rare animals, helping researchers estimate their numbers. Some large animals wear a tracking collar that sends their location by satellite, revealing how far they travel. This information has shown the importance of wildlife corridors, strips of protected land that connect separate forests, allowing animals to move, find food and breed.
Protecting certain animals benefits whole ecosystems. A keystone species, such as the elephant, shapes its environment by creating paths and spreading seeds. An apex predator like the tiger controls the numbers of herbivores, preventing them from destroying vegetation. When these animals disappear, the effects ripple through the entire system.
In some regions, conservation has moved beyond protection towards restoration. Rewilding projects aim to bring back native species and allow natural processes to recover. Zoos contribute through breeding programmes for endangered animals, while wildlife centres rehabilitate injured or rescued animals before returning them to the wild. These efforts show that, with enough commitment, decline is not inevitable.
